government.notes: Space policy is decided at presidential level by decree and executed by GGPEN under MINTTICS, with an interministerial commission coordinating ministries. Funding comes from the state budget approved by the National Assembly, historically combined with export credit and intergovernmental financing for satellites from Russia and France. The government announced in October 2025 that GGPEN will be converted into an Angolan Space Agency, but formal creation was not confirmed in this run. President Lourenço is in his final term, and the next general election is expected in 2027.

strategy.summary: Angola's National Space Strategy 2016-2025 was approved by Presidential Decree No. 85/17 and is implemented by GGPEN, the national space program management office under the telecommunications ministry. It is built on five axes: space infrastructure, training and promotion, industry and technology, international positioning, and organization and cooperation. Its horizon has passed and no successor strategy was found, though the government cited it in October 2025 when announcing the conversion of GGPEN into an Angolan Space Agency.

strategy.summary: The official CONAE page describes the Plan Espacial Nacional as a strategic plan, a state policy of national priority, with three components: Earth observation, peaceful exploration and use of outer space, and technological development for space use. The preliminary version 2016-2027 was approved by the CONAE Directorio and presented to the national executive (CONAE page, 2026). On 10 Dec 2025 the SICyT presented the Bases para el Desarrollo Espacial Argentino as a roadmap for a new plan, including a national space hub, a space-access project and an astronaut-training platform, and international value-chain integration. The full bases document was not found on the official site.
strategy.budget: No consolidated budget for the plan is published in the sources opened. Decree of Necessity and Urgency 867/2026, published in the Boletín Oficial on Friday 4 Sep 2026 (regional press, La Capital), increased CONAE resources for programmes and activities linked to space policy; the press report gives no amount. A press-reported real-terms cut of about 65 percent since December 2023 was not verified and is not used.
goals: Earth observation for Argentina's continental and maritime territory (CONAE plan axis)
Peaceful exploration and use of outer space, including cooperative missions (CONAE plan axis)
Technological development for space use and domestic industry (CONAE plan axis)
strategy.law: No comprehensive national space activities law was found. Ley 27208 (Ley de Desarrollo de la Industria Satelital; sanctioned 4 Nov 2015; Boletín Oficial 11 Nov 2015) declares the development of the satellite industry a matter of national interest and state policy (art. 1) and approves the Plan Satelital Geoestacionario Argentino 2015-2035 (art. 2). A 'Ley Espacial Argentina' bill appeared only in a search snippet; its PDF was not readable and it is not used.

strategy.summary: No standalone national space strategy document was found. The Prime Minister said on 10 Sep 2026 that the Government Programme 2026–2031 makes national space capabilities a standalone strategic objective. The stated goals are at least three national satellites (two Earth observation, one telecommunications), sovereign ground infrastructure, a distributed ground-station network and participation in international programmes. The legal basis is Law HO-152-N on Space Activity (6 Mar 2020), which sets Government approval of development and financing programmes and a Government-authorised state body. A science-sector programme 2026–2030 names space as a priority (PM release; not fetched).

Enable Armenian engineers and companies to contribute to international space programmes (PM release, 10 Sep 2026)

strategy.owner: Azercosmos (Space Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan)
strategy.summary: Space Strategy 2030 is published on the Space Agency website as the sector development path to 2030. Its three goals are economic growth and sustainable space development, a national space ecosystem based on research, and national interest through space projects. Priority directions include satellite service sustainability with replacement satellites, local production with a Spacecraft Development Center and at least 50 jobs, national security and backup links, and research, human capital, startups and SMEs. The strategy has no stated budget. Its predecessor is the 2009 State Programme on the Establishment and Development of the Space Industry.
strategy.budget: No budget for Space Strategy 2030 found in any fetched official source. Cabinet decision No. 106 (16 Apr 2026) changes a figure in clause 5.1 of the agency charter from 473 605 880 to 567 605 880; currency and purpose are not stated in the extracted text, so it is not recorded as a strategy budget. The seed USD 120 million satellite purchase (2023 press) is not re-proved.

Formation of a national space ecosystem based on scientific research and application of innovative solutions
Protecting national interests by implementing space projects for peace and prosperity

strategy.summary: Belgium has no single published long-term national space strategy document. Federal space policy is set through the Council of Ministers decision of 23 December 2025 on Belgian space programming for 2026 to 2030, which funded the ESA subscriptions made at the November 2025 Bremen ministerial and introduced defense co-financing of ESA participation. BELSPO designs and implements the policy around science, societal use, industrial development and economic return. The decision mandates a strategic review by 2028 to define future Belgian space policy.

strategy.summary: Bulgaria has no adopted national space strategy. In its 2025 statements to UN COPUOS the government said drafting a National Space Strategy and a National Space Program is its top short-term priority, alongside domestic space legislation and the creation of a national space agency. Space policy is coordinated by the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation, and in practice is framed by the European Cooperating State Agreement with ESA (renewed in 2022), EU space program participation, and the Artemis Accords (joined 2023). A draft update to the Innovation Strategy for Smart Specialisation 2021-2027 adds a national priority on space and dual-use technologies (public consultation closed 20 September 2026).

government.notes: Bahrain's space program is anchored in the security establishment. The Bahrain Space Agency is governed by a board and sits under the Supreme Defence Council, whose secretary general briefs the King on the agency's work. A general election is due in November 2026, which does not change the executive leadership.

The ABE 2026 accountability report says that until a 2026-2030 plan is approved, the PDES 2021-2025 is the medium-term reference, and the ABE enterprise plan 2021-2025 (Directorio Resolution 01/2022, 2 Mar 2022) is the programme reference. goals: Keep the TKSAT-1 satellite effectively occupied (medium-term action 1)
Maintain customer satisfaction for corporate and basic services (action 2)
Consolidate ABE as the State's strategic provider of Earth-observation services (action 3)
Maintain satellite service availability to international standards (action 4)
Implement a TTC station for lunar and deep-space missions (action 5)

strategy.law: DS 0423 (10 Feb 2010) creates ABE under MOPSV supervision. DS 0599 (18 Aug 2010) changes its legal nature to a public enterprise and Empresa Pública Nacional Estratégica. DS 4735 (8 Jun 2022) expands its functions (cited in the 2026 report; text not fetched).

strategy.summary: Brazil's space activities are guided by the National Policy for the Development of Space Activities (PNDAE) and implemented through ten-year National Programs of Space Activities. The current PNAE covers 2022 to 2031 and was approved at the end of 2021. The AEB is finalizing a new PNAE for 2027 to 2036, expected in 2026, which emphasizes national capacity and autonomy, space applications and integration of space technology into strategic sectors. The defense side follows the Strategic Program for Space Systems (PESE) of the Ministry of Defense.

strategy.budget: The 2019 strategy cites CAD 1.9 billion for the Gateway robotic system, CAD 150 million over five years for the Lunar Exploration Accelerator Program and CAD 100 million over five years for low Earth orbit broadband projects. Budget 2025 allocated CAD 182.6 million over three years for a sovereign launch program at National Defence, which in March 2026 committed a CAD 200 million ten year launch pad lease and CAD 105 million in Launch the North grants.
goals: Join the lunar Gateway with an advanced AI enabled deep space robotic system
Inspire young Canadians through a Junior Astronauts contest and outreach
Apply space to broadband connectivity, remote medicine, food access and security
Modernize space regulations and help commercial space firms start up and scale up
Renew the Canada and ESA cooperation agreement to 2030
Maintain leadership in Earth observation data, including continuity after the RADARSAT Constellation Mission
strategy.law: No comprehensive national space law. The Canadian Space Agency Act (1990) and the Remote Sensing Space Systems Act (2005) apply, and commercial launches are authorized case by case under an approach Transport Canada announced in 2023 while a dedicated regime is developed

strategy.summary: The 2019 strategy treats space as a strategic national asset and anchored Canada's AI enabled robotic contribution to the US led lunar Gateway, alongside commitments on youth, space applications, the commercial sector and space based data. strategy.summary: Chile's National Space Policy was approved by Supreme Decree No. 30 of July 2024 and cleared by the Comptroller General in March 2025, succeeding the 2014-2020 policy. It rests on two central objectives, the sustainable development of national space capabilities and the integrated management of space for national security and socioeconomic progress, organized around six strategic axes. Implementation runs largely through the National Satellite System (SNSat) operated by the Chilean Air Force and the National Space Center in Cerrillos, which opened in December 2025.

strategy.summary: Colombia's most recent adopted space policy is CONPES 3983 of January 2020, which set enabling conditions for the space sector to support national productivity and competitiveness, with an action plan that closed in December 2021. It called for reforming the Colombian Space Commission, reducing barriers for private entry, filing orbit and spectrum resources with the ITU, and commercializing defense satellite capabilities. As of 2025 the Colombian Space Commission reported to UN COPUOS that it was drafting a new National Space Policy to define national space governance and institutions, and no successor policy had been identified as adopted by this date.

government.notes: Costa Rica has a space law but no operating space agency in the sources opened. Law 9960 (Creación de la Agencia Espacial Costarricense, expediente 21.330; sanctioned 26 Mar 2021; Alcance 106 a La Gaceta 102, 28 May 2021) makes MICITT the rector for science and technology and chairs the AEC board. A repeal bill (expediente 25.795, 22 Sept 2026) is in committee and reports that the executive director post was never filled and the board last met in Q1 2023. Defence and finance space bodies were not researched beyond the Finance Ministry's joint role in Law 9960. The MICITT minister is not named here: the presidency gabinete page is dated 2023 and conflicts with 2026 press.

strategy.summary: Approved by the government in October 2025, the plan sets the long-term vision for Czechia as an active and internationally recognized space actor that uses space technologies for the economy, society and security. It defines seven strategic goals and seven competence platforms, from satellites up to 500 kg and scientific instruments to Earth observation data processing and space security and defense. It also frames the national Czech Path to Space project, including a Czech astronaut mission to the ISS expected around 2027 to 2028. Coordination of space activities moved from the Ministry of Transport to the Ministry of Industry and Trade on 1 March 2026.

strategy.summary: Germany's national space strategy was adopted by the federal cabinet on 27 September 2023, replacing the 2010 strategy, and treats space infrastructure as critical infrastructure for Germany and Europe. It sets nine fields of action ranging from European and international cooperation and New Space growth to security, sustainability, research and exploration. Since 2025 federal civil space policy has been consolidated in the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR), which told the Bundestag in November 2025 that a decision on rewriting the strategy will follow once its new space department is fully established. A separate Space Security Strategy was presented in cabinet in November 2025.

strategy.summary: Spain has no single adopted national space strategy. Its civil space policy rests on the Spanish Space Agency (AEE), created by Royal Decree 158/2023 under the joint authority of the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities and the Ministry of Defense, and on the 2022 Aerospace PERTE investment plan. On the security side, the 2019 National Aerospace Security Strategy, adopted under the National Security Council, still frames policy. In 2023 the science minister set a Space Law and a National Space Plan as AEE objectives, and the government has committed 455 million euros a year to ESA through 2030.

strategy.title: Ghana Space Policy
strategy.horizon: No end year stated. The policy's implementation matrix sets timelines from 1 year to 5 years.
strategy.owner: Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation (MESTI); implementation by GSSTI and GAEC
strategy.summary: The policy sets a national framework for space science and technology (SST): establishing a Ghana Space Agency, space education, infrastructure, research, applications and commercialisation, international collaboration, a legal and regulatory framework, and outreach. It was approved by Cabinet in March 2022 and unveiled in November 2024. It states the policy 'will be coordinated by' MESTI.
strategy.budget: No appropriated amount found. Policy target: 'Allocate at least 0.1% of GDP for SST activities', with annual budget support for the national space agency and an SST development fund (policy Section 5, Financing; Ministry of Finance named as the responsible body in the implementation matrix).
goals: Establish the Ghana Space Agency as a national entity with legal authority
Space education and human resource development
Build space infrastructure, including ground stations and research centres
Promote space science research and development
Space application and commercialisation of space products
Collaboration with relevant local and international organisations
Legal and regulatory framework, including ratification of the five UN outer space treaties
Space science outreach, education and awareness in schools and to the public
strategy.law: No space act enacted found. The policy (section 4.1.7) commits Ghana to put space laws and regulatory systems in place and to ratify the five UN outer space treaties. Legislation for the Ghana Space Agency is being drafted after Cabinet approval (GNA, 3 Oct 2026; Graphic Online, press conference 5 Oct 2026); no parliamentary stage found. Constitutional authority: Article 58(1) vests executive authority in the President.

other_docs.note: Announced by the Minister on 2 Oct 2026 (GSSTI news; GNA 3 Oct 2026). Graphic Online reports the press conference of 5 Oct 2026. Dates differ across outlets; the approval itself is consistent.

strategy.summary: Greece presented its first National Space Strategy, running to 2030, together with the HELLAS-SPACE 2.0 program at the Greece in Orbit event on 26 June 2026. The strategy follows the first phase national microsatellite program funded through the Recovery and Resilience Facility and ESA, and shifts emphasis from participation in European programs to domestic production and technological autonomy. It sets five national goals and includes a governance system with annual progress reviews. HELLAS-SPACE 2.0 targets national production lines and international tenders with at least 50 percent Greek participation.

strategy.summary: Hungary adopted its first national space strategy in 2021, aiming to use the space sector as a driver of innovation and growth, to strengthen the country's international role, and to build the knowledge base and infrastructure for the sector. Its flagship projects were national satellite and ground segment capabilities and the HUNOR astronaut program, which flew a Hungarian astronaut to the ISS on Axiom Mission 4 in June 2025. strategy.summary: Indonesia's space policy rests on Law No. 21 of 2013 on Space Activities and the 2017 presidential master plan that sets long term targets to 2040 for space science, remote sensing, space technology, launch and commercial space activities. Since the former space agency LAPAN was merged into the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) in 2021, space research and implementation sit inside BRIN. The master plan is evaluated every five years, and BRIN officials stated in early 2026 that some targets need to be redefined to be more adaptive and realistic. Current priorities are a national spaceport at Biak, Papua, and domestically built Earth observation satellites focused on food security.

strategy.summary: Approved at the 29th COMINT meeting on 14 May 2026, the DSPSN is Italy's first comprehensive national planning framework for space and implements the Government Guidelines on Space and Aerospace approved by COMINT in late 2024. It sets priorities for the next decade along four axes: research and benefits for society, industrial competitiveness, governance and regulation, and international cooperation. It treats space as a domain of strategic competition and calls for a national space security strategy, a critical space technologies plan and operational security and defense capabilities. It operates within Law No. 89 of 2025 on the space economy.

strategy.budget: The Space Strategy Fund at JAXA targets about 1 trillion yen over ten years, with 0.8 trillion yen secured as of 2025 (Cabinet Office, 2026). JAXA's annual budget was 215.5 billion yen in fiscal 2023.
goals: Ensure space security, including space domain awareness and resilient satellite systems
Strengthen national resilience and address global issues through Earth observation, positioning and communications
Create new knowledge through space science and exploration, including Artemis lunar participation
Strengthen the industrial and technology base, including H3 launch capability
Double the space industry market from 4.0 trillion yen (2020) to 8.0 trillion yen in the early 2030s
Expand the QZSS regional navigation constellation to seven and later eleven satellites
strategy.horizon: 10 year plan with a 20 year outlook, roadmap revised annually
strategy.law: The Basic Space Act (2008) is the framework law. The Space Activities Act (2016) licenses launches and satellite control, and the Diet passed an amendment in June 2026 that extends licensing to rocket launches generally, adds pre launch certification of space objects and broadens operator liability, with human spaceflight and reusable vehicles left to later rules. The Remote Sensing Data Act (2016) and the Space Resources Act (2021) are also in force.

strategy.summary: The 4th Basic Plan, decided by the National Space Committee on 21 December 2022, covers 2023 to 2027 and frames the goal of becoming a major space economy power by 2045. It is implemented through annual plans by the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), founded in May 2024 under the Ministry of Science and ICT. A July 2026 National Space Committee meeting accelerated lunar lander timelines and set a domestic LEO communications network target for 2035. The next five-year basic plan is due to cover the period from 2028.

strategy.summary: Luxembourg's national space strategy for 2023 to 2027 is set by the Ministry of the Economy and implemented by the Luxembourg Space Agency (LSA). Its central theme is sustainability, organized around economic sustainability, sustainability of activities on Earth and in space, and the responsible use of space resources. It aims to grow and diversify the space sector as part of the national economy, backed by ESA participation, the national LuxIMPULSE program, and dedicated finance instruments. The strategy horizon ends in 2027, so a successor document is due.

strategy.title: Programa Espacial Mexicano 2026-2030
strategy.owner: Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones (ATDT), with the Agencia Espacial Mexicana as technical authority
strategy.summary: Published in the DOF on 4 June 2026 with the ATDT as issuing body, under the Plan Nacional de Desarrollo 2025-2030 and the ATDT sectoral programme. Its legal basis cites CPEUM arts. 26 and 28, the Ley de Planeación and the 28 Nov 2024 DOF decree that created the ATDT. Initial projects: a new national telecommunications satellite to connect remote localities; a constellation of small Earth-observation satellites; a national centre to process satellite imagery; specialist training; and international cooperation, including ITU coordination of orbital positions and spectrum. The AEM is the technical authority, and the programme states that the AEM had not yet produced a current strategic programme in its institutional phase.
strategy.budget: No dedicated budget figure for the 2026-2030 programme is stated in the programme text. Press (Expansión, 8 Jan 2026, citing the 2026 PEF) reports a federal allocation to the AEM of 46,755 millones de pesos, down 33.1% from 69,950 millones in 2025. The unit and the PEF annex are not verified; a separate press report gives a different scale. Treat as press-reported, unit unresolved.
goals: Build a new national telecommunications satellite to connect remote localities
Deploy a constellation of small Earth observation satellites for civil protection, environment, agriculture, security and territorial planning
Create a national centre to process and analyse satellite imagery from national and commercial systems
Train Mexican specialists for the space sector
Link Mexico to the international space sector and strengthen management of orbital positions and spectrum rights at the ITU
strategy.law: No comprehensive national space activities law found in the sources opened. Founding statute: Ley que crea la Agencia Espacial Mexicana (DOF 30 Jul 2010), which creates the AEM as a decentralised public body; its 2010 sector reference (SCT) is superseded by the ATDT sectorisation stated in the 2026 programme. Constitutional basis: CPEUM art. 28 (satellite communication as a priority area under State rectory) and art. 26 (planning).

strategy.title: National Space Science and Technology Policy (2021)
strategy.status: in force (implementation period 2021/22 to 2029/30; reaffirmed by government, Mar 2026)
strategy.owner: Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sport, Arts and Culture (implementation lead); NCRST (coordinating agency). Issued in 2021 by MHETI.
strategy.summary: Namibia's Cabinet adopted the policy on 23 March 2021 (Cabinet no. 4TH/23.03.21/006), launched 4 June 2021. It has four objectives: awareness; collaboration and funding; human and institutional capacity; access and use of space technology. Cabinet approved drafting a Space Science and Technology Bill in 2025 (press). A national steering committee ran public consultations in 2026 (NBC). No enacted law or space agency was found; the government reaffirmed the policy in March 2026.
strategy.budget: The policy's implementation plan (appendix) has a budget column in N$ thousands per activity; the totals were not extracted. No separate national space budget line was found in the sources opened. The 2026/27 education budget (press) includes N$25.5m for a satellite data ground receiving station at the Windhoek Telecom earth station, a separate site; not confirmed as space budget in an official document. NUST station: government-funded (SIA, Mar 2026), amount not stated.
goals: Improve awareness and appreciation of space science and technology in Namibia (Objective 1)
Ensure collaboration and mobilisation of resources for funding space science and technology (Objective 2)
Build human and institutional capacity in space science and technology (Objective 3)
Ensure optimal access to and use of space technologies (Objective 4)
strategy.law: No space law enacted in sources opened. Space Science and Technology Bill: Cabinet approved drafting (Aug 2025, press); National Steering Committee consultations in 2026 (NBC). Not tabled in Parliament as far as found. Legal basis of NCRST: Research, Science and Technology Act, 2004 (Act 23 of 2004), as cited in the 2021 policy.

strategy.summary: Nigeria's National Space Policy was approved in 2000, and a 25-year implementation roadmap was endorsed in 2005, phased from government-funded development toward commercialization and public-private partnership. Several targets slipped, including a first Nigerian astronaut (originally 2015, later restated for 2030) and a full launch capability. strategy.summary: The Long-Term Space Agenda, prepared on the advice of the Netherlands Space Office and endorsed by the cabinet in February 2025, replaced the earlier three-year policy cycle tied to ESA ministerial conferences. It sets six missions spanning security, climate, science, satellite data, industry and international law. A 2017 to 2024 policy evaluation found the missions insufficiently concrete, and in January 2026 the cabinet committed to prioritize them. The Netherlands Space Office was renamed the Netherlands Space Agency in March 2026 with a stronger mandate.

government.notes: Space policy and regulation sit in one portfolio, with the Minister for Space acting as both policy lead and statutory licensing decision-maker, advised by MBIE and the New Zealand Space Agency (led by an acting General Manager, Space, Andrew Johnson, per the August 2026 briefing). Funding is small and largely flows through MBIE appropriations, Cabinet reprioritizations and the Catalyst Fund rather than a dedicated space budget. Security agencies screen license applications and the 2025 amendment added national security powers over ground stations. The portfolio changed hands twice in 2026 (Chris Penk from 7 April, Paul Goldsmith from 13 August), and a general election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 with official results due 27 November 2026, so the incumbent Luxon government continues until a new government is formed.

strategy.summary: Oman's National Space Policy and Executive Program is a ten year framework for 2023 to 2033 that aims to make Oman a regional hub for space applications. It rests on four pillars (economic diversification, national security, capacity building and environmental stewardship) and prioritizes the downstream sector as the entry point. Implementation runs in three phases, from preparation and legal frameworks, to priority projects, to expansion and sustainability, through 14 key projects and 8 quick wins. The ministry reported that 2023 to 2025 achievements included growth to about 26 space companies and over 400 sector jobs.

strategy.summary: Pakistan's first National Space Policy was approved by the federal cabinet in December 2023 and sets the country's first legal and regulatory framework for space activities. It frames space as a tool for socioeconomic development and national security, commits to peaceful use, and opens the market to public-private partnerships and foreign low Earth orbit communications providers. SUPARCO implements, monitors and revises the policy, and the Pakistan Space Activities Regulatory Board licenses operators under rules issued in 2024. The policy sits beside the longer running Space Program 2040, which drives a fast satellite launch cadence built mainly with Chinese partners.

strategy.summary: Peru has no adopted national space policy. In July 2024 the Ministry of Defense formally launched the formulation of a Política Nacional Espacial, with CONIDA leading the process and technical advice from the ministry's General Directorate of Policy and Strategy, and in November 2025 CONIDA was still contracting analysis to support the drafting. strategy.summary: The Philippine Space Act, approved on 8 August 2019, embeds the Philippine Space Development and Utilization Policy and created the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) as the central body for space policy and programs. The policy aims to make the country space-capable and space-faring within a decade, organized around six key development areas. Implementation runs through PhilSA, whose Director General holds Cabinet rank and serves as Presidential Adviser on Space Matters, with the Earth observation satellite MULA as the current flagship mission expected to launch in late 2026.

strategy.summary: Portugal Space 2030 was approved by the Council of Ministers on 15 February 2018 together with the draft Space Law, and set the national strategy for space to 2030. It aims to grow a space economy built on data, services and infrastructure, using the Atlantic position of the Azores for launch, return and ground station activities. In 2025 the government set up a Space Interministerial Working Group that shaped a record ESA subscription, and the 2026 agenda centers on the Santa Maria spaceport, reentry operations and the Atlantic Constellation with Spain. No formal successor strategy had been published as of this file.

strategy.summary: Rwanda's National Space Policy, dated March 2025, sets the goal of a resilient space sector by 2035 that contributes to economic growth and quality of life. It is organized around the principles Build, Grow, Collaborate and Inspire and six policy areas (economic development, international cooperation, education and capacity building, sustainability and self-reliance, regulatory framework, governance). The program is civilian led and implemented mainly through the Rwanda Space Agency, which regulates and coordinates national space activities.

strategy.summary: Singapore has not published a national space strategy document. The policy basis is the mandate of the National Space Agency of Singapore (NSAS), established on 1 April 2026 under the trade and industry ministry, which took over the Office for Space Technology and Industry (OSTIn) and has five pillars: national space capabilities, R&D, industry, international partnerships and space legislation. Operational guidance comes from the 2024 Guidelines for Singapore Related Space Activities, and funding from the S$210 million Space Technology Development Program set aside since 2022. Official statements say Singapore does not prioritize launch capability because of land constraints.

government.notes: Serbia has no space agency, so space decisions run through the Government and individual ministries, with the Ministry of Science as the de facto lead and funder through its research budget. International commitments are driven by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Artemis Accords, 2026) and sector bodies (RHMZ for EUMETSAT, BioSense for Copernicus). The political setting is in flux: President Vucic resigned on 27 September 2026 to run for Prime Minister, Speaker Ana Brnabic is acting President, the National Assembly is dissolved ahead of the 25 October 2026 snap election, and a presidential election must follow within three months. Prime Minister Djuro Macut (in office since 16 April 2025) leads the government until a new one is formed.

strategy.summary: Serbia has no dedicated national space strategy, space law or space agency. Space activity is handled through general science and innovation policy, chiefly the Strategy of Science, Technological Development and Innovation 2026 to 2030 adopted by the Government on 3 September 2026, which does not single out space. The main policy signals are accession to the Artemis Accords (signed by the Foreign Minister at NASA Headquarters on 16 July 2026), the Ministry of Science funded MOSAIC CubeSat led by the Astronomical Observatory of Belgrade, and Copernicus and EUMETSAT cooperation arrangements. No ESA cooperation agreement was found.

government.notes: The Riksdag sets space appropriations in the annual budget, with civil space funds channeled through the Ministry of Education and Research to the Swedish National Space Agency and military space funds through the Ministry of Defence. Recent space decisions have been issued jointly by the Education, Defence and Finance ministries. Kristersson asked to be released after the left-leaning opposition won a narrow majority in the September 2026 election and leads a caretaker government. On 15 October 2026 the Riksdag rejected Magdalena Andersson as prime minister by 248 votes to 99, and government formation was still ongoing as of 23 October 2026.

strategy.budget: ESA CM25 subscription of EUR 305 million, 1.36 percent of the ESA total, of which EUR 138 million to optional programs. The agency's 2027 to 2029 budget request proposes SEK 2.08 billion for appropriation 3:4 Space research and space activities in 2027, rising to about SEK 2.95 billion in 2029. The 2026 spring amending budget added SEK 400 million, with SEK 386 million in equity for SSC launch capability at Esrange and SEK 14 million for licensing at the Swedish National Space Agency. Military space is funded separately through the Armed Forces space billion for 2024 to 2032 and a SEK 1.3 billion military satellite package announced in January 2026.
goals: Promote peaceful and sustainable use of space and help develop international rules, including on space debris
Make space data easily accessible across society, including EU navigation and Earth observation services
Use state space activity to strengthen national security and military capability
Make critical infrastructure resilient to disruption of space services and extreme solar storms
Keep space legislation supportive of domestic activity, international obligations and private investment
Keep participation in ESA and EU programs predictable and strengthen industry competitiveness
Maintain Esrange in Kiruna as a key national and European resource and sustain high quality space research
strategy.horizon: not specified
strategy.law: Act on Space Activities (Lag om rymdverksamhet, SFS 1982:963) remains in force. A new space law is in preparation but no bill had been presented as of this date. In May 2026 the Swedish National Space Agency was tasked with preparing a new licensing organization as a first step.

strategy.summary: The government communication of 9 May 2018 sets a long-term platform for Swedish space activities, with benefit to society at the center while national security is safeguarded. It covers international cooperation, use of space data, security and critical infrastructure, legislation, industry competitiveness, Esrange, research and skills. It is complemented by the 2024 Defence and Security Strategy for Space, and a new space law is in preparation.

government.notes: Space policy is set by the National Space Policy Committee, chaired by a Deputy Prime Minister with the digital economy ministry providing the secretariat, and its decisions go to the Cabinet for approval. Implementation and most space funding sit with GISTDA and NARIT under the higher education and science ministry, through the annual budget act passed by parliament. Spectrum and orbital filings are handled by the independent NBTC. Following the 8 February 2026 general election, the House re-elected Anutin Charnvirakul as Prime Minister on 19 March 2026 and the King endorsed his second cabinet on 31 March 2026.

strategy.summary: Executive Order 14369, signed on December 18, 2025, sets national space policy across civil exploration, national security, commercial development and space nuclear power. It fixes deadlines for a crewed Moon return and a permanent lunar outpost, directs the Secretary of War to implement a space security strategy, and gives commercial solutions preference in federal space acquisition. It revoked EO 14056 and with it the National Space Council, placing coordination with the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology.

strategy.summary: Decision 169/QD-TTg, signed by the Prime Minister on 4 February 2021, sets Vietnam's space science and technology strategy through 2030 and builds on the 2006 national space technology strategy. It targets a mid-level position in space science and technology in Southeast Asia by 2030, mastery of small high-resolution Earth observation satellite technology, replacement of the VINASAT communication satellites and a large expansion of the space workforce. At the March 2026 inauguration of the Vietnam National Space Center, the government restated these targets and said it is moving toward a national space law.

strategy.summary: Presidential Decree 85/17 of 10 May 2017 approves the Estratégia Espacial da República de Angola 2016-2025 (Diário da República I Série n.º 76, p. 1657). strategy.budget: No budget figure in the strategy text. Section II.6 says ANGOSAT and human-resource projects are funded through the General State Budget (OGE) and that financing is to be identified in future; no amount found.
goals: Define the state's strategic axes and macro measures for the space sector up to 2025
Guide space activities centrally to avoid dispersion and duplication of effort
Use outer space as a development instrument and to strengthen Angola's international position
Ensure Angola's independence in services, products, technologies and human resources in the space sector
Ensure sustainability and stability of space investment
Ensure transparency and predictability of Angolan space activities
strategy.law: No dedicated national space law was found. The legal basis is presidential decree: Decree 85/17 approves the strategy (cites Constitution arts. 120(b) and 125(3)); GGPEN was created by Decree 154/13 of 9 Oct 2013 (strategy text, section I).

strategy.title: No single long-term national space strategy document found. Operative instrument: Belgian Space Programming 2026-2030 (Programmation spatiale belge pour la période 2026-2030), Council of Ministers decision of 23 Dec 2025
strategy.horizon: 2026–2030 programming; strategic review of future Belgian space policy by 2028
strategy.owner: Federal Council of Ministers, on the proposal of the Minister for Science Policy (Vanessa Matz); BELSPO implements; Defence co-finances ESA participation
strategy.summary: No single published long-term national space strategy document was found on the BELSPO or federal pages fetched; BELSPO's "Belgian space strategy" page describes policy in general terms. The operative decision is the Council of Ministers programming of 23 Dec 2025 for 2026–2030: it takes note of the November 2025 ESA ministerial, approves the ESA subscriptions and Defence co-financing (EUR 400 million set aside in the multiannual budget), mandates a BELSPO–Defence protocol, and requires a strategic review of future Belgian space policy by 2028 with attention to economic return and regional balance.
strategy.budget: Federal communication (19 Dec 2025): a Belgian contribution of EUR 1.1 billion for the 2026–2030 period. BELSPO debriefing (9 Dec 2025) gives a total Belgian space level of 1,845 M€ for 2025–2030 (1,277 M€ + 168 M€ defence participation + 400 M€ one-off) and about EUR 335 million per year to ESA incl. the defence contribution. Council decision: EUR 400 million set aside in the multiannual budget. Defence: GALO constellation "more than EUR 200 million" (press-reported, 16 Jul 2026; official defence document not found). Defence investment programmes 2026–2034: EUR 617 million (BELSPO deck). Reconciliation of the 1.1 bn and 1,845 M€ figures is not proved.
goals: Fund Belgian subscriptions to the ESA programmes agreed at the November 2025 ministerial (Council decision approves the subscription)
Co-finance Belgian ESA participation with Defence under a BELSPO–Defence protocol, aligned with NATO spending targets where possible (protocol mandated)
Strengthen Belgium's position in ESA's European Resilience from Space programme (mandate to the minister)
Keep ESEC at Redu as ESA's reference centre for cybersecurity (mandate)
Seek more Belgian staff at ESA and a Belgian director post at the next renewal (mandate)
Complete a strategic review of future Belgian space policy by 2028, considering economic return and regional balance
strategy.law: Act of 17 September 2005 on activities of launching, flight operations or guidance of space objects, as consolidated after the revision of 1 December 2013 (Moniteur belge 15 January 2014). It requires authorisation by the Minister for Science Policy and provides for a national registry. Consolidated copy from BELSPO; amendments after 2013 and the status of a draft replacement implementing decree (reported in 2021) were not verified.

strategy.title: Exploration, Imagination, Innovation: A New Space Strategy for Canada
strategy.status: under revision (a replacement is being prepared; a Special Adviser on Space was appointed 21 Oct 2026)
strategy.horizon: No fixed end date in the 2019 document; dated commitments include the ESA agreement to 2030 and LEAP funding over five years
strategy.owner: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (Minister of Industry), delivered largely through the Canadian Space Agency
strategy.summary: The 2019 strategy names space a strategic national asset and sets five priorities, the first being Canada's contribution to the US-led Lunar Gateway. It commits CAD 1.9 billion to an AI-enabled deep-space robotic system, CAD 150 million over five years to the Lunar Exploration Accelerator Program, and renews the ESA cooperation agreement to 2030. CP24 reported on 21 Oct 2026 that the Minister of Industry described a new space strategy in preparation at SpaceBound 2026, and the Prime Minister named astronaut Jeremy Hansen as Special Adviser on Space on 21 Oct 2026. No replacement strategy text has been published in the sources opened.
strategy.budget: The 2019 strategy commits CAD 1.9 billion to the Gateway robotic system and CAD 150 million over five years to LEAP; a 2018 announcement (cited in the strategy) provided CAD 100 million over five years for LEO broadband. National Defence committed CAD 200 million for a 10-year launch pad lease and CAD 105 million in Launch the North grants in March 2026. No replacement strategy budget is published.
goals: Ensure Canada remains a leading spacefaring nation by joining the Lunar Gateway mission
Inspire the next generation of Canadians to reach for the stars
Harness space to solve everyday challenges for Canadians

strategy.status: in force (Comptroller record 26 Mar 2025; cited as updated in the 2025 UN statement)
strategy.horizon: Not stated in the policy text read.
strategy.owner: Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation (MinCiencia), with the Consejo de Política Espacial and the Comité Ejecutivo Espacial
strategy.summary: Approved by supreme decree (No. 30, 4 July 2024, per DO Decree 28 of 2025). Two central objectives: sustainable development of national space capabilities (research, advanced technology, talent and international cooperation), and integrated management of space for national security and socioeconomic progress. Six strategic axes: 1 cooperation and linkage with society; 2 talent management; 3 innovation and development; 4 sustainable development; 5 security and sovereignty; 6 territorial planning. The Air Force's Sistema Nacional Satelital and the satellite centres are the operational vehicles named in the policy and in DO Decree 28. The Chilean statement to the UN (2025) reports the policy update and the Artemis Accords.
strategy.budget: No consolidated public space budget is stated in the policy text (MinCiencia PDF) or in DO Decree 28 of 2025. Funding is described as coming through ministry lines; this is not verified against the budget law (sourced absence of a space budget figure).
goals: Sustainable development of national space capabilities in research, innovation and advanced technology
Talent formation and training for the space sector
Mastery and national development of advanced space technologies
International cooperation and linkage with society in space
Integrated management of space for national security and socioeconomic progress, through national space systems
Connection and exploration of the whole national territory with national space systems
strategy.law: No dedicated national space activities law was found in the sources opened. Ley 21.105 (creating MinCiencia) gives the ministry the duty to promote space activity, coordinated with the Ministry of Defence (art. 4 m, quoted in DO Decree 28 of 2025). The policy lists the UN space treaties to which Chile adhered by decree: DS 818/1977 (liability), DS 987/1981 (Moon Agreement), DS 76/1982 (rescue and return), DS 77/1982 (outer space principles).

strategy.title: Política de Desarrollo Espacial: Condiciones Habilitantes para el Impulso de la Competitividad Nacional (CONPES 3983)
strategy.status: expired (horizon ended December 2021); successor National Space Policy in drafting per the 2025 COPUOS statement; no adopted successor found
strategy.horizon: Implementation to December 2021 (CONPES 3983, section on horizon)
strategy.owner: DNP as CONPES technical secretariat; participating entities include DNP, DAPRE, MinRelaciones, MinDefensa, MinTrabajo, MinComercio, MinTIC, IGAC and MinCiencias. The CCE is drafting the successor policy.
strategy.summary: CONPES 3983, approved on 13 January 2020, sets a space policy whose purpose is to create enabling conditions so that space technologies raise productivity, diversification and sophistication of the economy. It rests on three axes: a long-term strategic vision, measures to identify barriers to private entry, and a governance framework. The 2025 Colombian statement to COPUOS says the CCE is drafting a National Space Policy; no adopted successor was found in the sources opened.
strategy.budget: Estimated total cost COP 1,904 million (1.904 millones de pesos) for 2020-2021, per CONPES 3983 (table on financing by year). No current national space budget found.
goals: Generar las condiciones habilitantes y el entorno institucional para el sector espacial (CONPES 3983 objective)
Establecer una visión estratégica de largo plazo para el sector espacial (first axis)
Identificar barreras de entrada para el sector privado y proponer una hoja de ruta (second axis)
Definir un marco de gobernanza y articulación entre instancias (third axis)
strategy.law: Decreto 2442 de 2006 creates the Colombian Space Commission, amended by Decreto 184 de 2023 (the President or representative presides). Ley 2302 de 2023 (12 July 2023) adopts measures to guarantee defence and territorial integrity in the space sphere. Decreto 1064 de 2024 (23 Aug 2024, MinDefensa) regulates controlled space activities. No comprehensive national space law found.

strategy.title: National Space Plan 2026-2032 (Národní kosmický plán 2026-2032, NKP 2026+)
strategy.owner: Government of the Czech Republic; drafted under the Ministry of Transport, administered by MPO since 1 Mar 2026
strategy.summary: Fourth national space plan, approved by the government on 22 Oct 2025 and following the 2020-2025 evaluation presented on 25 Jun 2025. States that the Czech Republic is an active space actor and sets four priority areas: strategic lines and competence platforms; perspective technologies; the supporting space ecosystem and use of space data; institutionalisation, including a Czech Space Agency by end-2032.
strategy.budget: Indicative financing table in NKP Annex 6 (CZK million): total 3,170 in 2026 and 2027, then 2,370 a year for 2028-2032. ESA mandatory activities 400 a year; ESA optional programmes minimum 1,470 a year. Government Resolution No. 365 of 21 May 2025 requires a CZK 1,600 million contribution for the ISS mission in 2026-2027. Amounts are indicative. The seed's 'CZK 2 billion over three years' is not in the plan; press reports give about CZK 2 billion as the total mission cost.
goals: Priority area 1: define strategic development lines and create competence platforms (NKP section 4.1)
Priority area 2: support perspective space technologies (section 4.2)
Priority area 3: strengthen the supporting space ecosystem and use space data for the economy and society (section 4.3)
Priority area 4: institutionalise space activities, including a Czech Space Agency by end-2032 (section 4.4)
strategy.law: No national space act identified. The NKP text cites no space act. The e-Sbírka legal database could not be searched in this run (site content not readable), so this absence is provisional.

strategy.title: Raumfahrtstrategie der Bundesregierung ("Neue Wege für die Raumfahrt")
strategy.status: adopted by cabinet 27 Sep 2023; renewal under review (Drucksache 21/2796, 13 Nov 2025); no newer strategy adopted in fetched sources
strategy.horizon: Not stated in the fetched text
strategy.owner: Federal Government; policy run by BMFTR Department R (space policy and industry, sub-division R1)
strategy.summary: The 2023 national space strategy sets nine priority areas: European and international cooperation with ESA as core framework; space as a high-tech and New Space market; climate, resources and environment; digitalisation and downstream use; security and strategic capacity; sustainable use of outer space; space research; international exploration; and space dialogue and talent. The government said on 13 Nov 2025 that a decision on a new strategy would follow full integration of the BMFTR structures. The first federal space security strategy was presented in cabinet on 19 Nov 2025.
strategy.budget: About EUR 7.5 billion for BMFTR space in this legislative period, stated by the minister in the Bundestag (bulletin 22 Apr 2026, "knapp 7,5 Milliarden Euro in dieser Legislaturperiode"). 2026 government draft space lines (Drucksache 21/2796): BMFTR EUR 137 m; BMWE EUR 1,287 m; BMV EUR 345 m. Draft figures; enacted 2026 budget not checked.
goals: Strengthen European and international cooperation, with ESA as the core framework.
Grow space as a high-tech and New Space market, including launch and small satellite companies.
Use space data for climate, environment, digitalisation and downstream applications.
Secure strategic capacity to act and protect space infrastructure as critical infrastructure.
Promote sustainable use of outer space, including debris mitigation.
Sustain space research, exploration and talent recruitment.
strategy.law: No German space activities act found in force. Cabinet key points (Eckpunkte) for a Weltraumgesetz adopted 4 Sep 2024 (BT-Drs. 20/12775). Per the official lobby register (industry entries of June and 27 Jul 2026), a national space law is in inter-ministerial coordination (Ressortabstimmung); no BMFTR or BMWE draft (Referentenentwurf) was found published as of 27 Oct 2026.

strategy.title: Estonian Space Policy and Programme 2020–2027 (Eesti kosmosepoliitika ja -programm 2020–2027)
strategy.status: published policy and programme; adopting act not located; the ministry page links it as current policy
strategy.owner: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM); delivered by the Estonian Space Office in EIS
strategy.summary: The programme sets a vision of Estonia as a strong partner in European space programmes, with strengths in space services for decision-making, autonomous robotics and space cybersecurity. Its aims are to grow high-tech entrepreneurship, exports, the local space industry, education and research. It sets an ESA funding target of EUR 10 million a year by 2027, against EUR 2.7 million in 2019. ESA acts as procurement agency until a national structure exists (MKM). The adopting act (government order or ministry decision) was not located in this run.
strategy.budget: Programme cost table totals EUR 90,780,000 for 2020–2027 (Annex 1). The text says the realistic full cost will be under EUR 80 million because the funding target will not be reached from 2020. No state budget appropriation verified in this run.
goals: Public sector and public services: space services centre and use of space data
Technology entrepreneurship and space industrial policy
Education and science in space
International cooperation, with ESA and the EU space programme

strategy.title: Space Strategy 2030 (Avaruusstrategia 2030)
strategy.owner: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment (TEM) with the Finnish Space Committee
strategy.summary: Renewed national space strategy, Publications of the Finnish Government 2025:8, dated 21 January 2025. Vision: "Finland 2030: World's most advanced space operating environment, which generates benefits for society as a whole." Four objectives: utilisation, operating environment, capabilities and international role. Prepared by a working group under the Committee's Secretary-General and steered by the Committee; the Committee monitors implementation. No repeal found in this run.
strategy.budget: No budget total in the strategy text. The measures are defined against "the economic constraints and the resources available for the work" (section 3). Seed figures (EUR 233m ESA CM25; EUR 158m ICEYE SAR contract) are not proved and are not in the file.
goals: Utilisation: use space services to streamline and secure activities in all areas of society
Operating environment: Finland as an inspiring, secure and predictable environment for space actors
Capabilities: Finland can produce and utilise space services and has the capabilities to do so
International cooperation: Finland as a reliable, sought-after and active actor in the space sector
strategy.law: Act on Space Activities (Laki avaruustoiminnasta 63/2018), in force from January 2018; licensing, supervision and registration are laid down in it (strategy section 2). The Act on Earth Stations and Certain Radars (96/2023) is also cited. A 2026 government draft (VN/9441/2025) would move space licensing from TEM to Traficom; it is a consultation draft, not enacted in any source opened.

Not a budget law or annex; no budget document opened.

Rethink the industrial and commercial model of space industries
Rethink strategic and defence space capabilities
Adopt a more offensive approach to space science and exploration
Relaunch European space through competitiveness, European preference and new governance

strategy.title: UK Space Strategy
strategy.horizon: Spending review period to 2030 with longer-term goals to 2035 (strategy text)
strategy.owner: UK Space Agency, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade and Ministry of Defence (joint publication; BIST and MOD coordinate cross-government framework)
strategy.summary: The UK Space Strategy, published 8 Sep 2026 and updated 15 Sep 2026, sets out the UK approach to space with defence, national security and economic growth at its centre. It is backed by more than £7.8 billion of funding to 2029/30 and has a plan to 2030 under the spending review and goals to 2035. Strategic oversight sits with the Cabinet-level National Security Council; BIST and MOD coordinate a cross-government framework; a ministerially chaired Space Industry Advisory Group was set up in May 2026.
strategy.budget: More than £7.8 billion to 2029/30 (strategy text). Activity envelopes for 26/27 to 29/30 stated in the strategy: SatCom £2.8 billion (including Defence Satellite Communications £2.3 billion); Space Discovery £1.295 billion; Earth observation and meteorology £990 million; Space Ecosystem £706 million (including MOD novel technologies £420 million and National Space Innovation Programme £65 million); Space Domain Awareness £274 million; Assured Access to Space £227 million; in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing (ISAM) £117 million.
goals: Be a competitive space power, assertive in protecting UK interests and driving growth (strategy vision)
Put defence, national security and economic growth at the centre of the UK approach
Strengthen collective defence through NATO, sharing capabilities and supporting assured access to space
Pro-growth regulation that protects orbital and terrestrial environments and enables safe operations
Scale up commercial space businesses and deliver assured and nationally separable capabilities
By 2035: a leading in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing (ISAM) industry; assured UK launch access; nationally separable space control and SDA
strategy.law: Space Industry Act 2018 and Outer Space Act 1986 (legislation.gov.uk; both up to date with changes known to be in force on 27 Oct 2026). The CAA administers the Space Industry Act 2018 licensing regime; the Act schedule proves CAA charging, and the annex names the CAA as reforming orbital licensing.

strategy.title: Rencana Induk Penyelenggaraan Keantariksaan Tahun 2016-2040 (National Space Master Plan, Perpres 45/2017)
strategy.status: in force (effective on promulgation, Pasal 6; no revocation seen in the sources opened)
strategy.horizon: 2016-2040 (25 years, Perpres 45/2017 Pasal 1; UU 21/2013 Pasal 40(4)); review at least every 5 years (Pasal 5)
strategy.owner: President (sets the master plan on the proposal of the minister who coordinates the agency, UU 21/2013 Pasal 40(5)); prepared by the space agency (Lembaga), now BRIN per BRIN pages and news reports
strategy.summary: Presidential Regulation 45/2017 sets the 2016-2040 national space master plan with a vision, mission, policy, strategy and short, medium and long-term targets by five-year period (Lampiran, pp. 48-49). It is the national reference for space activity (Pasal 3). Under Pasal 4 the agency head monitors implementation and reports to the President through the minister for research and technology. The plan is reviewed at least once every five years (Pasal 5).
strategy.budget: No budget figure in Perpres 45/2017. UU 21/2013 Pasal 89 names the funding sources: state budget (APBN), grants, private sector and international cooperation. No national space budget amount was opened in this run.
goals: Five-year targets 2016-2040 for space science, remote sensing, space technology, launch and commercial space activity (Perpres 45/2017, Lampiran pp. 48-49)
Launch services from national territory and own-rocket satellite launch capability in 2036-2040 (Perpres 45/2017 Lampiran, p. 48)
Build and operate a national spaceport (bandar antariksa) under UU 21/2013 Pasal 44 (agency builds and operates it)
Biak spaceport: BRIN plans 100 hectares for technical facilities in 2026 (Bisnis.com, 7 Jan 2026; news report, not a regulation)
strategy.law: Law No. 21 of 2013 on Space Activities (UU 21/2013 Keantariksaan), read in the Ministry of Finance legal database copy. Master plan at Pasal 40; funding at Pasal 89; the government must issue the implementing presidential regulation within two years (Pasal 104(2)).

strategy.title: Indian Space Policy 2023
strategy.horizon: Not stated in the policy text (seed targets for 2035, 2040 and a USD 44 billion economy by 2033 are not in the policy and are NOT proved)
strategy.owner: Department of Space (nodal department, policy para 8), approved by the Union Cabinet
strategy.summary: Cabinet-approved policy that opens space activities to non-government entities through IN-SPACe. It sets the vision of a flourishing commercial presence in space, promotes R&D, public goods, a predictable regulatory framework and start-up support, and makes the Department of Space the nodal department. ISRO, IN-SPACe and NSIL have distinct roles in the policy text.
strategy.budget: Notes on Demands for Grants 2026-2027 (Budget Division, Feb 2026), Demand No. 95 Department of Space, page 313: Budget 2026-2027 gross INR 13,705.63 crore (revised 2025-26: 12,448.60). Within it: ISRO BE 2026-27 INR 194.57 crore; IN-SPACe BE 2026-27 INR 43.00 crore (same PDF, Demand 95 detail). The seed Antariksh Venture Capital Fund figures are NOT re-proved.
goals: Augment space capabilities and develop a flourishing commercial presence in space (policy vision, para 2)
Encourage advanced R&D in the space sector (policy para 3.i)
Provide public goods and services using space technology for national priorities (policy para 3.ii)
Create a stable and predictable regulatory framework for non-government entities through IN-SPACe (policy para 3.iii)
Promote space education, innovation and support for space start-ups (policy para 3.iv)
strategy.law: No enacted national space statute found in this run. Authorisation of non-government space activity rests on Indian Space Policy 2023 and IN-SPACe guidelines (policy para 5). The Space Activities Bill: secondary reports (2025) describe a draft finalised in May 2025 and under inter-ministerial consultation; no official source for introduction in Parliament was retrieved (see flags).

strategy.title: National Space Strategy for Enterprise 2019-2025
strategy.status: expired (horizon 2025); successor in preparation, scoping only (DETE, 20 Mar 2026); no successor text published
strategy.owner: Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (then Department of Business, Enterprise and Innovation)
strategy.summary: National space strategy for enterprise adopted in 2019, aimed at growing space-active Irish companies' participation in ESA and EU programmes. The fourth progress report (published Mar 2026, covering 2024) says 15 of 19 priority actions are achieved and others are ongoing. DETE said on 20 Mar 2026 that preparatory work on the next iteration has begun with a preliminary scoping exercise. A fifth and final progress report is under way.
strategy.budget: No separate budget line for the 2019-2025 strategy was opened. The government committed EUR 32.17m in 2024, including a core funding allocation of EUR 26.17m (progress report pp. 5, 8). Ireland's EUR 170m ESA commitment to 2030 was agreed in Nov 2025 (DETE, 20 Mar 2026).
goals: Double the space related revenue and employment in space-active Irish companies (by 2025)
Support 100 companies to benefit from ESA engagement (116 achieved by end 2024, per progress report)
Double the value of contracts won through EU Horizon programmes in space-related activities
Increase industry, public and international awareness of space and Ireland activities in space
Develop and attract talent for space-active and related industries
Develop a sustainable Earth Observation services sector based on advanced data analytics
strategy.law: No Irish national space activities statute was identified in the official sources opened. The 2019 strategy (p. 32) gave the Space Enterprise Coordination Group the role of considering an appropriate legislative framework; the 2025-2026 DETE consultation concerns the EU Space Act proposal. This is an unverified absence: a statute-register search was not completed.

strategy.title: Documento Strategico di Politica Spaziale Nazionale (DSPSN), National Space Policy Strategic Document
strategy.status: approved by COMINT at its 29th meeting (session 14 May 2026, reported by ASI 15 May 2026); full text not located on the official sites opened
strategy.horizon: Medium to long term (ASI page). The ten-year horizon and 15-year funding reported in press are not verified.
strategy.owner: COMINT (approves), prepared by ASI in coordination with COMINT; COMINT sits at the Presidency of the Council of Ministers (Law 89/2025 Art. 2)
strategy.summary: The COMINT approved the National Space Policy Strategic Document (DSPSN), prepared by ASI, which sets the national strategic framework for the sector in the medium-long term with objectives, priorities and lines of action: security and resilience of space infrastructure; competitiveness of the industrial supply chain; research; skills; strategic autonomy; and Italy’s international projection (ASI, 15 May 2026). It implements the government guidelines on space and aerospace approved in 2025 (ASI wording "lo scorso anno") and sits within Law 89/2025, whose Art. 22 requires a national space economy plan of at least five years, approved by COMINT and updated every two years.
strategy.budget: Statutory: Fondo per l’economia dello spazio, EUR 35 million endowment for 2025 in the MIMIT budget (Law 89/2025 Art. 23). ESA: Italy’s commitment at the ESA Council at Ministerial level 2025 is EUR 3.5 billion over three years, +13.5% on the previous ministerial (ASI Annual Report 2025). Press only (not proved as a primary budget): a government headline of EUR 7.8 billion to 2028 for the space plan, which L’Espresso reports as partly already allocated and spent. PNRR and PNC splits from the seed are not re-proved.
strategy.law: Law No. 89 of 13 June 2025, "Disposizioni in materia di economia dello spazio" (space economy law), Gazzetta Ufficiale Serie generale n. 144 of 24 June 2025, in force the day after publication (Art. 31). It defines ASI and COMINT (by reference to Art. 21 of d.lgs. 128/2003, as amended), creates the national authorisation regime for space activities, the national space economy plan (Art. 22) and the space economy fund (Art. 23). Implementing decrees (Art. 13 and others) were not verified.
goals: Strengthen security and resilience of national space infrastructure (ASI, 15 May 2026)
Increase competitiveness of the industrial supply chain (ASI, 15 May 2026)
Enhance research, develop skills and strengthen strategic autonomy (ASI, 15 May 2026)
Consolidate Italy’s international projection (ASI, 15 May 2026)

strategy.title: Dasar Angkasa Negara 2030 (National Space Policy 2030, DAN2030)
strategy.owner: Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (MOSTI), implemented through the Malaysian Space Agency (MYSA)
strategy.summary: DAN2030 is the national space policy under which MOSTI and MYSA implement space programmes to 2030. MOSTI said on 28 Sep 2021 that DAN2030 programmes were expected to contribute at least RM3.2 billion or 0.3 per cent of GDP by 2030, with 5,000 new jobs and a RM40 million a year satellite data market. In Aug 2026 MYSA's director-general cited a 2023 study of about 79 firms contributing at least RM6.21 billion and projected RM10 billion and about 5,000 jobs by 2030 (Bernama). The seed claim of a 1 per cent of GDP target is not supported by the sources opened and is removed. The DAN2030 document itself was not opened.
strategy.budget: No dedicated national space budget figure is verified. The MOSTI ministry-wide Budget 2027 figure of RM1.29 billion in the seed was not re-verified; the MOSTI portal lists a Budget 2027 debate item (26 Oct 2026) without the figure.
goals: Contribute at least RM3.2 billion or 0.3 per cent of GDP by 2030 (MOSTI, 28 Sep 2021 statement, via MOSTI-hosted press clipping)
Create about 5,000 new space jobs by 2030 and a RM40 million a year satellite data market (MOSTI, 28 Sep 2021)
Raise the space sector contribution to RM10 billion and about 5,000 jobs by 2030 (MYSA director-general, Bernama, 5 Aug 2026)
Select a national launch site, with operations expected around 2029 (seed; not re-verified)
strategy.law: Malaysian Space Board Act 2022 (Act 834). Royal assent 19 Jan 2022 and gazetted 25 Jan 2022 (MOSTI Act 834 Malay PDF). Section 1(2): the Act "comes into operation on a date to be appointed by the Minister by notification in the Gazette" (English PDF). MOSTI lists a commencement notice PU(B) 524 'Penetapan Tarikh Kuat Kuasa'; its date was not extracted (the PDF gave no readable text). The seed date of 1 Jan 2025 is not verified.

strategy.title: Long-Term Space Agenda (Lange-termijn ruimtevaartagenda, LTR)
strategy.horizon: 10–15 years, per the 27 Jan 2026 letter
strategy.owner: Coordinating minister (EZK), with the Stuurgroep NLSA (EZK, OCW, IenW, Defence)
strategy.summary: The LTR, dated January 2024, sets six missions for security and defence capacity, climate and living environment, scientific leadership, satellite data for society, economic opportunities for Dutch companies, and a strong international legal framework. The cabinet response of February 2025 created the Interdepartmental Council for the Space Domain (IRR). A 2017–2024 policy evaluation (completed July 2025) found the missions insufficiently concrete, and the cabinet letter of 27 Jan 2026 commits to prioritising them. The Netherlands Space Office became the Netherlands Space Agency (NLSA) on 3 March 2026. The LTR is a policy framework; no statute was found for it.
strategy.budget: ESA subscriptions for 2026–2028 of EUR 450.3 million at MC25: EUR 167.8 million mandatory and EUR 282.5 million optional, including a one-off EUR 109 million top-up (EUR 85 million from EZK, EUR 24 million from Defence). No separate LTR budget line was opened. The seed's '2.6 percent of the ESA total' is not used because the letter gives a 22.3 billion euro package, which does not support it.
goals: Build security and defence capacity in and through space (LTR mission 1)
Use space for climate and the living environment (LTR mission 2)
Maintain scientific leadership in space research (LTR mission 3)
Apply satellite data to societal challenges (LTR mission 4)
Create economic opportunities for Dutch companies in the space sector (LTR mission 5)
Strengthen the international legal framework for space use (LTR mission 6)
strategy.law: Wet ruimtevaartactiviteiten (Space Activities Act), Act of 24 January 2007, Staatsblad 2007, 80; consolidated text BWBR0021418 in force 1 July 2025 to present. Licensing by RDI (telecommunications act).

strategy.title: New Zealand Space and Advanced Aviation Strategy 2024–2030
strategy.owner: Minister for Space; Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (New Zealand Space Agency)
strategy.summary: Government strategy (September 2024) to double the size of New Zealand space and advanced aviation sectors by 2030. It sets five objectives, including developing sovereign space capabilities through a national space mission (objective 1), a world-leading regulatory environment (objective 2) and an aerospace-capable workforce (objective 4). MBIE pages retrieved 27 October 2026 still describe it as the government strategy.
strategy.budget: No dollar budget appears in the strategy document (text checked 27 Oct 2026). The seed figures (NZSA baseline NZD 3.75m a year, NZD 5.85m Tāwhaki reprioritisation, Catalyst NZD 9m and NZD 6m) are not verified and are not stated as fact here.
goals: Double the size of New Zealand’s space and advanced aviation sectors by 2030
Develop sovereign space capabilities through a national space mission (objective 1)
Establish a world-leading regulatory environment for space and advanced aviation (objective 2)
Build an aerospace-capable workforce (objective 4)
Deepen international partnerships, including the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom and Australia (seed; partner list not re-verified)
strategy.law: Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act 2017 (primary legislation for launches, launch facilities, high-altitude vehicles, ground-based space infrastructure and payloads; MBIE Our Act page). The 2025 amendment act (seed: assent 25 July 2025, in force 29 July 2025) is NOT verified: the MBIE Our Act page says statutory review recommendations are still being considered, and legislation.govt.nz returned HTTP 202 with no body.

goals: Position Oman as a regional gateway for space applications and services (programme page)

strategy.law: No space law in force. MTCIT has begun drafting an Omani Space Law and supporting regulations (Oman Observer, 27 Sep 2026, citing the ministry's 2023–2025 report); no enactment date has been announced. strategy.title: National Space Policy (Pakistan)
strategy.status: approved by federal cabinet 13 Dec 2023 (secondary: IBA; Dawn reprint). The policy PDF on SUPARCO site is headed "Draft prepared by" SUPARCO; entry into force "upon the date of its issuance". Cabinet date not on an official page.
strategy.horizon: National Space Program 2047 is named in the policy text as approved by the Government; the policy has no end date.
strategy.owner: Federal Cabinet (approval, secondary only); implemented by SUPARCO as National Space Agency (policy text)
strategy.summary: Pakistan's National Space Policy sets the national intent for outer space activities, names SUPARCO as implementing agency, and calls for a national legal and regulatory framework. The policy text on SUPARCO's site was read in this run; the goals below are taken from its Objectives section. Operational rules are set by the Pakistan Space Activities Rules-2024 (gazette). The cabinet approval date rests on secondary sources.
strategy.budget: SUPARCO Demand No. 096 (Development Expenditure of SUPARCO) in the FY2026-27 Details of Demands for Grants Vol. IV: Rs 4,895,000,000 voted for the year ending 30 June 2027; Rs 5,418,523,000 budget estimate for 2025-26. The budget-in-brief table also lists SUPARCO at 5,419 and 4,895 (Rs million). The PSDP line was not separately opened.
goals: Provide direction and supervision for space related activities in the country.
Enable promulgation of national legal and regulatory framework for the space sector.
Harness space science, technology and applications for socio-economic development and national security.
Support and sustain Pakistan's Space Program; encourage public-private partnership in the space sector.
Apply space technology to National and Sustainable Development Goals.
Promote local industry through spin-off technologies and strengthen the technological base.
Strengthen national and international cooperation and collaboration in the space sector.
strategy.law: Pakistan Space Activities Rules-2024 (S.R.O. 60(I)/2024), Rawalpindi, 1 Feb 2024, gazette extra. 2 Feb 2024, made by the National Command Authority under sections 15, 3(6) and 7(a) of the National Command Authority Act 2010 with Federal Government approval. Rule 4 names SUPARCO as National Space Agency; Rule 7 makes SUPARCO PSARB's secretariat; Rule 8 gives the NCA the chairman nomination. No standalone space act was found.

strategy.title: Philippine Space Development and Utilization Policy (Republic Act No. 11363, Philippine Space Act)
strategy.status: in force (takes effect 15 days after publication, Sec. 29; no repeal seen in the text read)
strategy.horizon: Within the next decade of enactment (RA 11363 Sec. 4); the Act sets no dated target year
strategy.owner: Congress (statute); implemented by the Philippine Space Agency under the Office of the President; policy body is the Philippine Space Council (President as chair)
strategy.summary: RA 11363, approved 8 Aug 2019, is the primary strategic roadmap for space development (Sec. 4). It sets six key development areas (Sec. 5): national security and development; hazard management and climate studies; space research and development; space industry capacity building; space education and awareness; and international cooperation. It creates PhilSA (Sec. 9-10) and the Philippine Space Council (Sec. 13). Its funding comes from the Philippine Space Development Fund (Sec. 22).
strategy.budget: FY2026 General Appropriations Act (DBM): PhilSA total new appropriations PHP 1,136,900,000. Statutory Philippine Space Development Fund: PHP 10 billion over five years from the national government share of PAGCOR and BCDA gross income (Sec. 22(a)), plus PHP 2 billion a year to PhilSA (text).
goals: National security and development through space applications (Sec. 5)
Hazard management and climate studies using space science and technology (Sec. 5)
Space research and development (Sec. 5)
Space industry capacity building through private-sector cooperation (Sec. 5)
Space education and awareness (Sec. 5)
International cooperation (Sec. 5)
strategy.law: Republic Act No. 11363 (Philippine Space Act), approved 8 Aug 2019 (Senate LRB text); in force 15 days after publication (Sec. 29).

strategy.title: Polish Space Strategy (Polska Strategia Kosmiczna)
strategy.owner: Council of Ministers (adopted by Resolution No. 6); coordination entrusted to the minister for the economy (§ 2)
strategy.summary: Adopted by Council of Ministers Resolution No. 6 of 26 Jan 2017 (M.P. 2017 poz. 203). Three strategic goals to 2030, including turnover of at least 3% of the European space market, public administration using satellite data, and access to satellite infrastructure for security and defence; five specific goals follow. POLSA's February 2024 evaluation recommends an update. No revised strategy was found in the sources opened.
strategy.budget: No strategy-specific budget line in the 2017 resolution. Related figures: (a) Act of 13 Feb 2026, Art. 73(1): state budget ceiling of PLN 28,150,000 for 2026-2036, of which PLN 3,210,000 in 2026, for the Act's tasks; (b) ESA: Poland declared nearly EUR 550 million for ESA optional programmes 2026-2028 at ESA Council (Bremen, Nov 2025), a state pledge, not a strategy line.
goals: Polish space sector competitive in the European market, at least 3% of overall European market turnover by 2030 (proportional to economic potential)
Public administration uses satellite data for faster and more effective tasks; domestic firms meet domestic demand and export
Polish economy and public institutions have access to satellite infrastructure, especially for security and defence
strategy.law: Act on Space Activities of 13 February 2026 (Ustawa o działalności kosmicznej), Dz.U. 2026 poz. 465; promulgated 3 Apr 2026; in force 18 Apr 2026 (Art. 74: 14 days after promulgation). POLSA President holds licensing and public-administration powers (Art. 6(1)); higher authority is the minister for the economy (Art. 6(3)); MON for units under its supervision (Art. 7); national register kept by POLSA President (Art. 44(2)).
